readerTitle: The manager who heard every word and missed the problem
caseNote: 가상 사례 (물류센터, B2B 소프트웨어) + 개념 출처 (Rogers & Farson, 1957 '적극적 경청')
insight: 경청은 조용히 듣는 태도가 아니라, 상대가 말한 단어 뒤의 상황을 확인해 이해했음을 보여주는 행동이다.
misconception: 말을 끊지 않고 고개를 끄덕이며 메모하면 잘 듣고 있는 것이다. 열린 문(open door) 정책이 있으면 경청하는 조직이다.

sources.text: Rogers, C. R. & Farson, R. E. (1957). Active Listening. Industrial Relations Center, University of Chicago.
물류센터와 소프트웨어 회사 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 'Active Listening' 논문의 저자(Carl Rogers, Richard Farson)와 발표 연도(1957), 발행처(University of Chicago Industrial Relations Center)를 게시 전에 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 연구 결과 수치 없이 개념 출처로만 언급했습니다.
물류센터의 스캐너·지게차 통로 사례와 소프트웨어 회사의 내보내기(export) 사례는 모두 가상입니다. 실제 사고 통계나 기업 사실은 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The manager who heard every word and missed the problem
body: Dana runs a busy distribution center. Her door is always open. Every month she holds a listening session with the night shift, says little, and takes careful notes.
For weeks, pickers told her the same thing: the scanners keep dropping out in aisle 14. She wrote it down every time. Then a forklift nearly hit a picker in that exact spot.

image.label: Warehouse aisle with a picker holding a scanner and a forklift approaching
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 물류센터 선반 통로 끝에서 작업자가 스캐너를 높이 들고 신호를 찾는 모습, 옆 통로에서 지게차가 다가오는 장면. 통로 기둥에 "14" 표시. 실제 기업 로고나 장비 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: "The scanners keep dropping out in aisle 14."
body: A picker says this to you at the end of a shift. You have five minutes before your next meeting.
What's your best response?

options.text: "Thanks for flagging it. I'll log a ticket with IT today."
options.feedback: Quick and polite, and the scanner may get fixed. But you've acted on the words without learning what the dropout actually causes on the floor.

options.text: "What happens when it drops out? Walk me through it."
options.feedback: It costs a few minutes, but you learn the real situation behind the complaint. That's where the risk was hiding.

options.text: "We're replacing all the scanners next quarter, so hang in there."
options.feedback: It sounds reassuring and saves time now. But it closes the conversation, and the picker learns that raising problems leads nowhere.

cards.title: She heard "scanner." They meant "danger."
body: Dana picked option A. IT marked the ticket low priority, since the scanners worked almost everywhere else.

What the pickers meant was different. When the signal dropped, they walked to the end of the aisle to rescan. The end of aisle 14 is the main forklift lane. A small tech glitch was pushing people into traffic many times a night.
Dana did everything that *looks* like listening. She just never asked the one question that would have turned the words into the real problem.

cards.title: Listening
body: **Listening** means working to understand what the other person means, and checking that you got it right, before you respond.

Psychologist Carl Rogers and Richard Farson called this *active listening* in a 1957 paper for managers. Their point: the listener's job is not just to receive words. It's to grasp the speaker's situation and show they've grasped it.
Silence and note-taking are a start. Understanding is the goal.

image.label: Speech bubble with the word 'scanner' and, behind it, a hidden scene of a forklift lane
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽에 말풍선 "Scanners drop out", 말풍선을 들추면 뒤에 숨은 장면(작업자가 지게차 통로로 걸어나가는 모습)이 보임. 위에 "What they said", 아래에 "What they meant" 라벨.

cards.title: Three moves that turn hearing into understanding.
body: Good listeners do a few simple things, in order:
list: **Ask for the story:** "Walk me through what happens." Specifics beat summaries.
**Reflect it back:** "So when it drops, you walk to the forklift lane to rescan?"
**Check what matters most:** "What worries you most about that?"
cards.callout: If they say "Yes, exactly," you've listened. If they correct you, you just avoided acting on the wrong problem.

cards.title: People judge listening by what they feel, not what you do.
body: Dana's team saw her nod and write. They never heard her say back what they meant, and nothing visible changed. So, from their side, she wasn't listening.
That has a cost beyond one aisle. When people feel unheard, they stop raising problems. The open door stays open, and fewer people walk through it.
The same pattern shows up with customers, suppliers and your own boss. A complaint is often a clue to a bigger situation the speaker hasn't fully described.

cards.title: Listening isn't agreeing, or promising.
body: You can understand someone fully and still say no. Saying "Here's what I heard, and here's why we're not changing it" respects them more than silent nodding.
It also takes time, so save the full version for problems that matter. And skip the scripts. Repeating "I hear you" without real questions feels hollow fast, and people notice.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: You run a B2B software company. On a call, the operations lead at one of your biggest customers says: "Your export feature is way too slow."
What do you say next?

options.text: "Got it. I'll have engineering make exports faster."
options.feedback: The customer feels heard for a moment. But you've committed engineering time to a guess, and speed may not be what they actually need.

options.text: "What are you doing when you need the export? Can you show me?"
options.feedback: You might learn they export every Monday to build a report for their boss. A scheduled report could solve that better than a faster export.

options.text: "Performance work is already on our roadmap. I'll send it over."
options.feedback: It's honest and shows progress. But it answers your plan, not their problem, so you still don't know what slow is costing them.

cards.title: You've listened when they say, "Yes, exactly."
body: Hearing the words is easy. Listening means asking for the story, saying it back, and checking you understood before you act.
**Try it today:** the next time someone brings you a problem, ask "Walk me through what happens" and then repeat it back in your own words before you offer a fix.
